solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Civil code maintained by Julian, say - and Lex?

blocks.note: Julian was a Roman emperor (and a Roman jurist), so 'say' marks him as an example of a Roman
lex is the Latin word for law

explanation.surface: A history lesson about who upheld the civil code in ancient times, ending with a nod to a man named Lex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lex' reads like a first name (Lex Luthor), but here it is the Latin noun. The whole clue also works as a description: Roman law was kept up by Romans, in Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman law is the civil code of ancient Rome, the basis of the civil-law systems of Europe.

clue.text: Dicky silly to include daughter in rural scenes

indicators.note: dicky means shaky or unsound, so the letters of 'silly' are in poor order

blocks.note: SILLY rearranged
d = daughter, the standard abbreviation, placed after the first letter of the jumble

explanation.surface: Someone called Dicky is behaving foolishly by bringing his daughter along into a country landscape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' looks like a man's name at the head of the sentence; in British English a dicky heart or knee is a weak one, which is why it signals rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Idylls are pictures, in verse or paint, of peaceful country life.

clue.text: Overindulging Miles during home redecoration?

blocks.note: papering walls is one way to redecorate a home; the '?' flags the example
m = miles, placed inside PA...PERING

explanation.surface: Someone called Miles is having too good a time while the house is being done up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miles' passes for a man's name, but it is only the abbreviation M, slipped into PAPERING.
explanation.definitionFit: Pampering someone is indulging them to excess.

clue.text: 13 Across representatives on coast at intervals after day in Calais

indicators.note: take every other letter of 'on coast', here the second, fourth and sixth
Calais is a French port, so 'day' is to be put into French

blocks.note: jour is French for day
o N c O a S t: the even-position letters

explanation.surface: Members of the press gather at a seaside spot shortly after a day in the French port of Calais.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 Across is PRESS, so its representatives are journalists; journo is the informal British and Australian word for one.
explanation.definitionFit: Journos are journalists, the people who represent the press.

clue.text: Naked tenants come in

indicators.note: stripped of its covering: the first and last letters come off

blocks.note: tenants are renters; 'naked' strips the first and last letters off that synonym

explanation.surface: A startling invitation for the people renting the flat to come inside without clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is to strip TENANTS itself, which gives the unhelpful ENANT; the synonym RENTERS has to come first.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: entering a room is coming into it.

clue.text: Load again on horse endlessly

indicators.note: the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: re = on, concerning
CHARGER, a war horse, without its final R

explanation.surface: A rider hoisting a pack back onto a horse that seems to go on for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: Recharging a gun or battery is loading it again, so the definition is fair beyond electricity.
explanation.definitionFit: To recharge is to load or fill again, as with a battery or a firearm.

clue.text: Moral values in English county mentioned by Mike Tyson?

indicators.note: the boxer Mike Tyson has a noted lisp, so any S he says comes out as TH

blocks.clueFragment: English county mentioned by Mike Tyson?
blocks.note: Essex said with a lisp, every S becoming TH

explanation.surface: A news item on the heavyweight boxer lecturing on morality in an English county.
explanation.walkthrough: Essex is a county east of London. The '?' admits the sound only works with Tyson's lisp.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethics are moral principles, the values that govern behaviour.

clue.text: Audacious form of dismissal reportedly

indicators.note: 'reportedly' means according to what people say, so the answer comes from the spoken sound of the phrase

blocks.note: in cricket a batter is out 'bowled' when the ball hits the stumps

explanation.surface: A cheeky way of sacking someone, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dismissal' suggests sacking, but in cricket it means getting a batter out, and bowled is one of the ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Bold and audacious both mean daring.

clue.text: Master and don excited receiving new decorations

indicators.note: stirred up, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, taken as printed
n = new, added to the fodder

explanation.surface: Two senior academics, a college master and a don, are thrilled to be handed fresh honours.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oxbridge surface makes 'decorations' look like medals or honours; in the answer it means ornaments.
explanation.definitionFit: Adornments are decorations, things added to make something look finer.

clue.text: Bound to accept essentially smallish current paper-maker's measure

indicators.note: the essence, the middle, of 'smallish'

blocks.note: a caper is a leap or bound; it opens as CA and closes as PER around the rest
smaLLish: the middle two of its eight letters
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A pair of odd claims about papermaking, sounding like a technical note on a small electric current.
explanation.walkthrough: In papermaking the calliper is the thickness of a sheet, so the word is the maker's measure as well as the tool that takes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Calliper is the paper trade's term for sheet thickness, measured with callipers.

clue.text: Cultural home husband returns to visit and so forth

blocks.note: at home = in
h = husband
etc = et cetera, and so forth; HNI goes between ET and C

explanation.surface: A husband coming back from abroad to visit his cultural roots, and so on.
explanation.walkthrough: Home giving IN is a crossword staple: to be in is to be at home. 'To visit' signals a container because a visitor goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethnic describes a group sharing a common culture or tradition.

clue.text: Where to spot those who are in form?

definitions.text: Where to spot those who are in form?

blocks.note: the surface reading: on good form, playing well
the setter's reading: pupils belonging to a form, the British school word for a group of pupils taught together

explanation.surface: A question about where to find athletes on a winning streak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In form' suggests people playing well; in British schools a form is a class or year group.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition by place: British schools call a group of pupils a form, and lessons gather them in one room.

clue.text: Insist on claim omitting nothing factual originally

indicators.note: these letters are left out of the word
the origin, the first letter, of 'factual'

blocks.note: to profess is to claim
o = nothing, removed
first letter of factual, also taken out of the claim word

explanation.surface: Someone insisting that a claim is true while leaving out the facts.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking 'Insist on' as the definition leaves 'claim' with no way in; only 'Insist' is needed, with 'on' as the link.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: pressing a point means insisting on it.

clue.text: Explain informal sandwich shop beneath Milan club

blocks.note: Inter Milan, the Italian football club
Pret A Manger is a British sandwich chain, called Pret for short

explanation.surface: A request for directions: the casual sandwich place underneath a football club's premises in Milan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Informal' marks the short name: Pret A Manger is a sandwich chain common in British cities.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym, as when a critic sets out what a poem means.

clue.text: Tense individual on BBC channel in black and white, typically

blocks.note: BBC Two is a British television channel
t = tense, as in grammar
one = a single individual

explanation.surface: A nervous person appearing on a BBC channel back in the black-and-white television days.
explanation.walkthrough: The blocks run in answer order: TWO first, then T and ONE. 'Typically' says black and white is just one example of two colours.
explanation.definitionFit: Two-tone means having two colours, and black and white is the classic pair.

clue.text: Happened to cut plant going over flowering shrubs

blocks.note: to set is to plant; turned over it is TES, split TE...S
arose = happened, occurred; sits inside TE...S

explanation.surface: A gardener's mishap: someone's cutting of a plant going wrong among the flowering bushes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' is a verb here: to set seeds or seedlings is to plant them.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea roses are a class of hybrid roses, flowering shrubs whose scent was likened to tea.

clue.text: Understanding hospital department twice close to collapse

indicators.note: the department appears two times
the closing letter of 'collapse'

blocks.note: ENT = ear, nose and throat
the department again
collapsE

explanation.surface: Two hospital departments reach an agreement just before the whole system falls apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to collapse' reads as nearly collapsing; here 'close' is the end of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: An entente is a friendly understanding between parties, as in the Entente Cordiale.

clue.text: One who's unfaithful to merit struggles, wife admitted

indicators.note: the letters wrestle into a new order

blocks.note: TO MERIT rearranged
w = wife, a standard abbreviation, let in after the first letter of the jumble

explanation.surface: A cheating spouse fights to deserve forgiveness, and the wife takes him back in.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a marital drama, fittingly for the answer: the wife is let in to make the cheat.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-timer is someone who cheats on a partner.

clue.text: Sound when shower starts? Mine excluded, not right!

indicators.note: the R, for right, is taken out

blocks.note: a pit is a coal mine
APART = excluded, set aside; without R it is APAT

explanation.surface: An exclamation about a noise when the rain begins, followed by an indignant protest at being left out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shower' suggests a bathroom, but it is a rain shower: the first drops go pitter-patter. The '?' marks the definition as a playful description.
explanation.definitionFit: Pit-a-pat is the light tapping sound of the first raindrops.

clue.text: Letters from Mandela backed flipping secret plot

indicators.note: the answer's letters are taken straight from the words that follow
those letters are turned end to end

blocks.note: the letters run across the gap between the two words, then read backwards

explanation.surface: Correspondence from Nelson Mandela supporting a scheme that keeps being turned around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed' looks like the reversal signal, but it is part of the hiding place; 'flipping' does the turning.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabal is a secret plot, or the small group of plotters behind one.

clue.text: Expression of assent finding rare primate

blocks.note: the sailor's doubled yes to an order from the captain
a nocturnal lemur of Madagascar, named for its call

explanation.surface: Someone nodding in agreement at the news that an unusual ape has been discovered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finding' reads as discovering, but it only links the two senses; one doubled word does both jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Aye aye is a naval yes, and the aye-aye is a rare nocturnal lemur.

clue.text: Size of US coin Poles first rejected

indicators.note: thrown back, so NO I reads ION

blocks.note: a dime is a US ten-cent coin
the north and south poles, N and S
first = number one, No. 1, written NOI; turned round it is ION

explanation.surface: A question about how big an American coin is, with Polish people refusing it first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like people from Poland, but it is the two compass poles. 'First' becomes No. 1, a less common trick worth learning.
explanation.definitionFit: A dimension is a measurement of size such as length or breadth.

clue.text: Tempted female golfer to lift protective cover

indicators.note: in a down answer, lifting turns the letters bottom to top

blocks.note: Eve, tempted by the serpent in Eden
Ernie Els, the South African golfer

explanation.surface: A woman golfer is tempted to raise the cover over her clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Female golfer' seems to go together as one person, but it is two: EVE, the female, and ELS, the golfer.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: record sleeves and cable sleeves both wrap and protect what is inside.

clue.text: Entertain male American in Anchorage on vacation

indicators.note: vacated, emptied of its middle, leaving just the outer letters

blocks.note: AnchoragE emptied: A...E
m = male, inside A...E
US = American, after M inside A...E

explanation.surface: Laying on fun for an American man holidaying in Alaska's biggest city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' reads as holidaying, but a vacated word is emptied, keeping only its ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: amusing people means keeping them entertained.

clue.text: Abandon criminality in favour of plugging rock band

blocks.note: R.E.M., the American rock band; FOR goes between RE and M
for = in favour of

explanation.surface: A rock band promoting a campaign to go straight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plugging' reads as promoting a record, but here it means filling a gap.
explanation.definitionFit: To reform is to give up crime and live lawfully.

clue.text: Order dessert course

definitions.note: 'apple-pie' stands for Order through the phrase 'apple-pie order', meaning perfect tidiness

blocks.note: as in the phrase for perfectly neat and tidy, '___ order'
a classic baked pudding with a fruit filling

explanation.surface: A diner asking the waiter for the pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' looks like a verb asking for the dessert; it is really a noun, the neatness of apple-pie order.
explanation.definitionFit: Apple-pie order is perfect neatness, and apple pie is a classic dessert.

clue.text: Science fiction concept perhaps developed adopting unknown colleague's tips

indicators.note: worked into a new form, so the letters of 'perhaps' are rearranged
the anagram takes in the extra letters
the two ends of 'colleague'

blocks.note: anagram fodder
y, one of the algebra unknowns
ColleaguE: its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A science fiction idea, maybe, worked up with help from an unnamed co-worker's suggestions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' seems to hedge the definition, as setters often do; here it is the anagram fodder. 'Tips' are ends, not advice.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyperspace is the sci-fi dimension through which ships travel faster than light.

clue.text: Challenge women's opinion

blocks.note: to vie is to compete, to challenge
w = women

explanation.surface: A call to take on what women think.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Women's opinion' seems to be one phrase, but the possessive only glues W to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: your view on a matter is your opinion of it.
